earlier_scan.source_named: Lu, Wen. 2018. Aspects of the Grammar of Tunxi Hui: A Transitional Sinitic Language (thesis); also Hirata 1998 Huizhou fangyan yanjiu. Not openly retrievable; Sinitic doculects described for tone rather than stress.

new_statements.quote: [p. 47] "As a typical Hui Chinese variety, Tunxi Hui has six citation tones and a very complex tone sandhi system." [p. 49] "When tone sandhi happens, it is exclusively the preceding tone in a disyllabic word or phrase that will change its tone value, a pattern known as right-dominant tone sandhi." [p. 54] "Neutral tones in Tunxi Hui, while they may be found, are not as evident or as common as in Mandarin. They only occur in functional words, such as some grammatical words such as the genitive marker and the perfective aspect marker, and sentence final particles, or the second reduplicated verb in a verb phrase."

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. Language not in catalog and no existing statements; this work supplies a first prosodic-type statement (tonal, six tones, right-dominant sandhi, toneless function-word syllables) but no word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tunxi Hui is described as a lexical-tone language: six citation tones (11, 44, 31, 24, 42, checked 5), extensive right-dominant disyllabic tone sandhi (the first syllable changes, the final syllable keeps its citation tone), and toneless 'neutral-tone' syllables restricted to function words (genitive ka, perfective, sentence-final particles, cliticized weak pronouns, second copy of a reduplicated verb), whose pitch is set by the preceding tone (p. 55). The thesis has no section on word stress and makes no statement about stress placement or its absence; the only uses of 'stress' are 'unstressed weak forms' for cliticized toneless pronouns (p. 125) and 'prosodically prominent' strong pronoun forms a24-le etc. 'in terms of not only volume and length, but also pitch and timbre' (p. 123).
new_statements.exceptions: Neutral (toneless) syllables only in function words and verb reduplicants; 'the neutral tones in Tunxi Hui are not always neutral' - realised approx. as low tone 1 after Tones 11/31/42 and higher tone 3 after Tones 44/24/5 (p. 55, after Qian 1997). Tone 11 splits into two sandhi classes by Middle Chinese origin (p. 48 n. 23).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Tunxi Hui 屯溪话 (Xiuyi subgroup of Hui Chinese, Tunxi district of Huangshan city, southern Anhui; ~70,000 speakers), largely following Qian (1997) for the tone system; huiz1242 'Hui Chinese' is the Glottolog language-level node covering all Hui varieties (Jixi, Yixian, Xiuning, Wuyuan etc. are other varieties with files in the same folder).

sources.note: Only modern full grammar of a Hui variety, in English, with a phonology chapter (consonants, vowels, 'a very complex system of tone sandhi'); the most likely place for an explicit statement on stress or its absence and on neutral-tone syllables. Licensed CC BY-NC-ND but the PDF is behind an automated-access block; needs a browser download.
